newsitem.title: UK: Unrest in the Balkans reminds world of tinderbox.
newsitem.headline: Unrest in the Balkans reminds world of tinderbox.

text.p: From Albania to Bulgaria and Serbia to Greece, passions are running high and showing the world once again that the Balkans remain unpredictable and explosive -- even if there is no longer a brutal war going on.

While much of Central and Eastern Europe seems stable and set on a course for political and economic integration with the West, poverty and politics in the Balkans have brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets in recent weeks.

Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, an autocratic ruler widely blamed for stoking the fires that brought collapse and war to Yugoslavia, is being challenged through mass protests by a vocal and increasingly confident opposition.

Albania, once a secretive Stalinist state, has been shaken by violence following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes. Bulgaria has been plunged into economic and political crisis, with demonstrators now trying to rid the country of a socialist government that was democratically elected.
Greece, although a member of the European Union, is still quarrelling with its traditional rival Turkey over the divided island of Cyprus and other issues.
In Bosnia itself, scene of Europe's worst conflict since the end of World War Two, hatred and mistrust still fester beneath the surface of a peace enforced by thousands of NATO troops.
Although the savagery of that war shocked the world, it brought home to outsiders just how different the Balkan region is and why it remains, in some senses, a place apart.

Burdened with an almost impossibly complex and violent history that is still very much a live issue, the Balkans are a breeding ground for nationalist, ethnic or religious fervour, often exploited by politicians.
All of this is poorly understood by outsiders who believe they have left such things behind in the late 20th century.
Western countries have been baffled by the strength of feeling displayed over place names or national symbols, most recently shown by the row between Greece and Macedonia.

The Balkans were the place where the Ottoman Empire, the high-water mark of Islamic influence in Europe, fought some of its great battles against Christianity, and where the 11th century Christian divide between the Orthodox and Catholic churches is still keenly felt.

The collapse and dismemberment of the Austro-Hungarian empire after World War One, a conflict that was itself touched off by assassination and political intrigue in the Balkans, did nothing to resolve those tensions.
Redrawing borders only provoked fresh animosity, created new problems with minorities and "ethnic cleansing" decades before anyone thought of the term.
Those conflicts were effectively bottled up during the Cold War, with everything dominated by the East-West confrontation.

Significantly, though, the biggest mavericks were in the Balkans. Yugoslavia was communist but non-aligned under Tito's rule, Albania quit the Warsaw Pact after a row with Moscow and Romania was the Soviet Union's most difficult ally.
Tito's death and the collapse of communist rule elsewhere allowed long-suppressed passions to resurface, with the added dimension that huge economic problems fed existing resentment.

While other countries like Poland and Hungary chose the path to the West, some Balkan states -- like Bulgaria and Romania -- stayed their own course and moved only slowly towards reforms. Yugoslavia disintegrated into five years of war.
